blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has published no examiners' comments for Paper 6; the guidance below comes from its suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.

**Two question types dominate.** The first is **MM and the arbitrage process** — a levered and an unlevered company of the same risk class, asking which is overvalued and how an investor profits. The second is **EBIT-EPS-MPS**: two or three ways of raising a given sum, judged on earnings per share and market price.
Every RTP in the set carries a question ICAI labels 'Capital Structure', and **MM appears in five of the eight**.

The 2-mark theory parts rotate through a short list: **optimum capital structure, over-capitalisation, pecking order theory, financial break-even and the EBIT-EPS-MPS relationship** — five topics that between them have appeared eight times in the MTPs alone.
May 2025 asked the pecking order hierarchy directly; May 2024 and May 2025 both set MM numericals.

blocks.title: How ICAI marks this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: In an EBIT-EPS question, **lay the alternatives out in parallel columns** — EBIT, interest, PBT, tax, PAT, preference dividend, earnings for equity, number of shares, EPS — exactly as the study material's Illustration 11 does.
**Recommend, don't just compute.** The final mark is for naming the better option and saying why, in one line.
In an MM question, always **value both firms first**, then say which is overvalued, then show the arbitrage steps — sell, borrow, invest, compare.
State your assumption where the question is silent on tax: the 1958 model has no tax, the 1963 model does, and the formulae differ.

concepts.title: 1. The Meaning of Capital Structure
understand: ==**Capital structure is the combination of capitals from different sources of finance.** The capital of a company consists of **equity shareholders' fund, preference share capital and long-term external debts**.==

**The source and quantum of capital is decided keeping three factors in mind.** **(i) Control** — the capital structure should be designed so that **existing shareholders continue to hold a majority stake**. **(ii) Risk** — it should be designed so that the **financial risk of the company does not increase beyond a tolerable limit**. **(iii) Cost** — the **overall cost of capital remains minimum**.

==**Practically, it is difficult to achieve all of the above three goals together**, hence a finance manager has to **make a balance among these three objectives**.== However, the objective of a company is to **maximise the value of the company**, and that is the prime objective while deciding the optimal capital structure.

==**Capital structure decision refers to deciding the forms of financing (which sources to be tapped), their actual requirements (amount to be funded) and their relative proportions (mix) in total capitalisation.**==

**The arithmetic that ties the chapter together.** ==**Value of the firm = EBIT ÷ Overall cost of capital (weighted average cost of capital)**==, and ==**Ko = (Cost of debt × weight of debt) + (Cost of equity × weight of equity) = [Kd × D ÷ (D + S)] + [Ke × S ÷ (D + S)]**==, where **Ko** is the WACC, **Kd** the cost of debt, **D** the market value of debt, **S** the market value of equity and **Ke** the cost of equity.

So the **capital structure decision will decide the weight of debt and equity and ultimately the overall cost of capital as well as the value of the firm**. Capital structure is therefore **relevant in maximising the value of the firm and minimising the overall cost of capital**.

**Whenever funds are to be raised to finance investments, a capital structure decision is involved.** A demand for raising funds **generates a new capital structure**, since a decision has to be made as to the quantity and forms of financing.
concepts.example: A company with EBIT of ₹1,00,000 and a WACC of 12% is worth ₹8,33,333. Drop the WACC to 11% and the same earnings are worth ₹9,09,091 — which is the whole reason the chapter exists.

expected_questions.question: Explain what is meant by capital structure, the factors that decide the source and quantum of capital, and how the capital structure decision affects the value of the firm.
answer_points: Capital structure is the combination of capitals from different sources of finance; the capital of a company consists of equity shareholders' fund, preference share capital and long-term external debts.

The source and quantum of capital is decided keeping in mind **control** — the structure should let existing shareholders continue to hold a majority stake; **risk** — financial risk should not increase beyond a tolerable limit; and **cost** — the overall cost of capital should remain minimum.

Practically it is difficult to achieve all three goals together, so a finance manager has to make a balance among them; the prime objective in deciding the optimal capital structure is to maximise the value of the company.

The capital structure decision refers to deciding the forms of financing (which sources to tap), their actual requirements (the amount to be funded) and their relative proportions (the mix) in total capitalisation.

Value of the firm = EBIT ÷ overall cost of capital, where Ko = [Kd × D ÷ (D + S)] + [Ke × S ÷ (D + S)]. The capital structure decision decides the weights of debt and equity, hence the overall cost of capital, and hence the value of the firm — which is why capital structure is relevant to maximising value and minimising cost.

concepts.title: 2–2.1 The Capital Structure Theories, and the Net Income (NI) Approach
understand: **Four approaches explain the relationship between cost of capital, capital structure and the value of the firm:** **(a) Net Income (NI) approach, (b) Traditional approach, (c) Net Operating Income (NOI) approach, (d) Modigliani-Miller (MM) approach.** The study material groups them as **relevance theories** (NI, traditional, and MM 1963 with tax) and **irrelevance theories** (NOI, and MM 1958 without tax).

**Seven assumptions** are made to understand the relationship: there are **only two kinds of funds — debt and equity**; the **total assets of the firm are given**, and the **degree of leverage can be changed by selling debt to purchase shares or selling shares to retire debt**; **taxes are not considered**; the **dividend payout ratio is 100%**; the **firm's total financing remains constant**; **business risk is constant over time**; and the **firm has perpetual life**.

**2.1 The Net Income approach.** ==According to this approach, the **capital structure decision is relevant to the value of the firm**. An **increase in financial leverage will lead to a decline in the weighted average cost of capital, while the value of the firm as well as the market price of the ordinary share will increase**. Conversely, a **decrease in leverage will cause an increase in the overall cost of capital and a consequent decline in the value as well as the market price of equity shares**.==
**Why.** **Ke and Kd are assumed not to change with leverage.** As debt — the cheaper source — increases, its greater weight **causes the weighted average cost of capital to decrease**.

**The arithmetic.** ==**Value of Firm (V) = S + D**, where **S** is the market value of equity and **D** the market value of debt. **Market value of equity (S) = NI ÷ Ke**==, where **NI is earnings available for equity shareholders** and **Ke the equity capitalisation rate**. ==**Overall cost of capital = EBIT ÷ Value of the firm.**==

==Under the NI approach the **value of the firm will be maximum at a point where the weighted average cost of capital is minimum**. The theory therefore **suggests total or maximum possible debt financing for minimising the cost of capital**, and its significant conclusion is that it **pleads for the firm to employ as much debt as possible to maximise its value**.==

**The study material's Illustration 1 pattern.** Rupa Ltd.'s EBIT is ₹5,00,000 with 10% debentures of ₹20 lakh and a given equity capitalisation rate. Deduct interest from EBIT to get earnings available for equity holders, divide by Ke to get S, add D to get V, and divide EBIT by V to get the overall cost of capital.
concepts.example: EBIT ₹5,00,000, interest ₹2,00,000 and Ke of 15% give equity worth ₹20,00,000; add ₹20,00,000 of debt and the firm is worth ₹40,00,000, so Ko = 5,00,000 ÷ 40,00,000 = 12.5%.

provisions.requirement: Ke and Kd constant; more debt lowers WACC and raises value; V = S + D, S = NI ÷ Ke, Ko = EBIT ÷ V; maximum debt is optimal.
provisions.exam_angle: The only theory that recommends 100% debt, which is what makes it examinable as a contrast.

official_questions.question: Theta Limited is expecting an annual earning of ₹3 lakh before paying any interest and taxes. The company has debt in its capital structure and a stated equity capitalisation rate. Compute the value of the firm and the overall cost of capital.
answer_points: **Under the Net Income approach (SM §2.1).** Earnings available for equity shareholders = EBIT − interest. **Market value of equity (S) = NI ÷ Ke.** **Value of the firm (V) = S + D.** **Overall cost of capital = EBIT ÷ V.**

**Under the Net Operating Income approach (SM §2.3), if that is what the question asks.** Value of the firm = EBIT ÷ Ko, with Ko given; **market value of equity = V − D**; and **Ke = earnings available for equity ÷ market value of equity**, which rises with leverage.
The two approaches give different answers from the same data, so the first line of the answer must name the approach being applied.

Where the question asks how the value changes if the debt is increased, the NI approach shows the value rising, while the NOI approach shows it unchanged — the contrast is usually the point of the question.
official_questions.conclusion: Name the approach, then run the four lines; the contrast between approaches is the examinable idea.

concepts.title: 2.2 The Traditional Approach
concepts.evidence: MTP 3 (Mar 2024 Series I, May 2025 Series I, Sep 2025 Series II)
understand: ==This approach favours that **as a result of financial leverage up to some point, cost of capital comes down and value of the firm increases; however, beyond that point, a reverse trend emerges**. The principal implication is that **the cost of capital is dependent on the capital structure and there is an optimal capital structure which minimises cost of capital**.==

**Three movements under this approach.** **(i)** The **rate of interest on debt remains constant for a certain period and thereafter, with an increase in leverage, it increases**. **(ii)** The **expected rate by equity shareholders remains constant or increases gradually; after that, the equity shareholders start perceiving a financial risk, and then from the optimal point the expected rate increases speedily**. **(iii)** As a result, the **WACC first decreases and then increases — and the lowest point on the curve is the optimal capital structure**.
==**Optimum capital structure occurs at the point where the value of the firm is highest and the cost of capital is the lowest.**==

**Where it sits among the theories.** According to the **net operating income approach, capital structure decisions are totally irrelevant**; **Modigliani-Miller supports the net operating income approach but provides behavioural justification**; ==the **traditional approach strikes a balance between these extremes**.==

**Main highlight.** The firm should **strive to reach the optimal capital structure and its total valuation through a judicious use of both debt and equity**. At the optimal capital structure, the **overall cost of capital will be minimum and the value of the firm will be maximum**.

**The study material's Illustration 3 and its warning.** Given options with different costs of debt and equity at debt ratios of 0.0 to 0.6, compute Ko for each and pick the lowest. ==The study material flags the trap expressly: **the ratio given is not the debt to equity ratio but the debt to total value ratio** — so a ratio of 0.6 means capital employed comprises **60% debt and 40% equity**.== In its own worked answer, Ko falls from 13.00% at zero debt to **12.80% at a debt ratio of 0.1**, then rises through 13.52%, 14.10%, 14.80%, 16.50% and 18.80% — so the **second option is the best because it has the lowest WACC**.
concepts.example: The study material's own table: 11% debt and 13% equity at a 10% debt ratio give Ko = 12.80%, the minimum. Push debt to 60% and both costs rise, taking Ko to 18.80%.

answer_points: **Note the base of the ratio first.** The ratio given is not the debt to equity ratio but the **debt to total value ratio**; a ratio of 0.6 means capital employed comprises 60% debt and 40% equity. Since the weights total 1 in every case, there is no need to divide by the total.

**Decision: the 2nd option is the best because it has the lowest WACC** of 12.80%. Under the traditional approach the optimum capital structure occurs at the point where the value of the firm is highest and the cost of capital is the lowest.
The pattern also demonstrates the theory: WACC falls as the first tranche of cheap debt is added, then rises once both Kd and Ke begin to climb with leverage.

concepts.title: 2.3 The Net Operating Income (NOI) Approach
concepts.evidence: MTP 2 (Mar 2024 Series I, May 2025 Series II)
understand: ==**NOI means earnings before interest and tax.** According to this approach, **capital structure decisions of the firm are irrelevant**. **Any change in the leverage will not lead to any change in the total value of the firm and the market price of shares, as the overall cost of capital is independent of the degree of leverage.** As a result, **the division between debt and equity is irrelevant**.==

**Why it works.** ==As per this approach, an **increase in the use of debt, which is apparently cheaper, is offset by an increase in the equity capitalisation rate**. This happens because **equity investors seek higher compensation as they are opposed to greater risk due to the existence of fixed return securities in the capital structure**.==
So in the diagram, **Kw (the weighted average cost of capital) and Kd (the debt capitalisation rate) are constant, and Ke (the cost of equity) increases with leverage**.

**The arithmetic.** ==**Value of the firm (V) = EBIT ÷ Ko**, with **Ko given**. Then **market value of equity (S) = V − D**, and **Ke = earnings available for equity holders ÷ market value of equity**, i.e. **(EBIT − interest paid on debt) ÷ S**.== Equivalently, ==**Ke = Ko(V ÷ S) − Kd(D ÷ S)**.==

**Illustration 4.** Amita Ltd.'s EBIT is ₹5,00,000, cost of debt 10%, debt ₹15,00,000 and overall cost of capital 15%. **V = ₹5,00,000 ÷ 0.15 = ₹33,33,333.** Interest = ₹1,50,000, so earnings available for equity = ₹3,50,000. **S = ₹33,33,333 − ₹15,00,000 = ₹18,33,333**, and **Ke = ₹3,50,000 ÷ ₹18,33,333 = 19.09%**.

**Illustration 5 — the two-company version ICAI keeps setting.** Alpha Ltd. has **50% debt and 50% equity**; Beta Ltd. has **20% debt and 80% equity**; both borrow at **8% in a no-tax world** with perfect capital markets and the same **net operating income of ₹3,60,000**, and Alpha's overall capitalisation rate is **18%**.

**Value of Alpha = ₹3,60,000 ÷ 0.18 = ₹20,00,000**, split ₹10,00,000 debt and ₹10,00,000 equity. Interest = 8% × ₹10,00,000 = ₹80,000, leaving **₹2,80,000** for equity, so a 2% holding returns **₹5,600** and the **implied required rate of return on equity is ₹2,80,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 = 28%**.

**Beta has the same value of ₹20,00,000**, split ₹4,00,000 debt and ₹16,00,000 equity. Interest = 8% × ₹4,00,000 = ₹32,000, leaving **₹3,28,000**, so its **implied required return on equity is ₹3,28,000 ÷ ₹16,00,000 = 20.5%**.

==**Why the difference?** The study material's own answer: Beta's implied required return on equity is **lower than Alpha's because Beta uses less debt**. As the **equity capitalisation is a linear function of the debt-to-equity ratio** under the NOI approach, **the decline in required equity return offsets exactly the disadvantage of not employing so much in the way of 'cheaper' debt funds**.==

official_questions.question: The capital structure of AN Ltd. in market-value terms is 50% debt and 50% equity. The borrowing rate for the company is 10% in a no-tax world and capital markets are assumed to be perfect. (i) If Mr. R owns 8% of the equity shares of AN Ltd., determine his return if the company has net operating income of ₹10,00,000 and the overall capitalisation rate of the company (Ko) is 20%. (ii) Calculate the implied required rate of return on equity of AN Ltd.
answer_points: **Earnings available to equity shareholders.** Net operating income ₹10,00,000 less interest on debt at 10% of ₹25,00,000 = ₹2,50,000, leaving **₹7,50,000**.
**(ii) Implied required rate of return on equity.** Earnings available for equity shareholders ÷ market value of equity = ₹7,50,000 ÷ ₹25,00,000 = **0.30, or 30%**.

Under the NOI approach, this 30% is higher than the 20% overall capitalisation rate precisely because equity investors demand compensation for the financial risk created by the fixed-return securities in the structure.
official_questions.conclusion: Value the firm, split it, deduct interest, divide — four steps in a fixed order.

official_questions.question: Zordon Ltd. has net operating income of ₹5,00,000 and total capitalisation of ₹50,00,000 during the current year. Compute the effect on the cost of equity and the overall cost of capital of different levels of debt in the capital structure.
answer_points: **Overall cost of capital.** Ko = EBIT ÷ total capitalisation = ₹5,00,000 ÷ ₹50,00,000 = **10%**, and under the NOI approach this stays at 10% whatever the level of debt.
**For each level of debt**, market value of equity (S) = total value less debt, and **Ke = (Net operating income − interest) ÷ S**.

As debt rises, the numerator falls by the interest and the denominator falls by the debt, and the study material's point is that **Ke rises just enough to keep Ko unchanged** — because the equity capitalisation is a linear function of the debt-to-equity ratio.
**Present the answer as a table** with columns for debt, equity, earnings available for equity, Ke and Ko, so that the constancy of Ko is visible across the rows.

Conclude with the approach's own words: any change in leverage will not lead to any change in the total value of the firm or the market price of the shares, as the overall cost of capital is independent of the degree of leverage.
official_questions.conclusion: A table across debt levels showing Ke rising and Ko flat is the whole answer.
keywords: independent of the degree of leverage

expected_questions.question: Alpha Ltd. and Beta Ltd. are identical except for capital structure. Alpha has 50% debt and 50% equity; Beta has 20% debt and 80% equity, both in market-value terms. The borrowing rate for both is 8% in a no-tax world and capital markets are perfect. Net operating income is ₹3,60,000 for each, and Alpha's overall capitalisation rate is 18%. (a) If you own 2% of Alpha's shares, determine your return, and calculate Alpha's implied required rate of return on equity. (b) Calculate Beta's implied required rate of return on equity and analyse why it differs.
answer_points: **Value of Alpha Ltd.** = NOI ÷ Ko = ₹3,60,000 ÷ 0.18 = **₹20,00,000**; market value of debt = 50% = ₹10,00,000 and of equity = 50% = ₹10,00,000.
**Return on a 2% holding in Alpha.** Net operating income ₹3,60,000 less interest of 8% × ₹10,00,000 = ₹80,000 leaves **₹2,80,000** for equity; 2% of that is **₹5,600**.
**Alpha's implied required rate of return on equity** = ₹2,80,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 = **28%**.

**Beta Ltd.** has the same total value of ₹20,00,000; debt = 20% = ₹4,00,000 and equity = 80% = ₹16,00,000. Interest = 8% × ₹4,00,000 = ₹32,000, leaving **₹3,28,000** for equity. **Implied required rate of return on equity = ₹3,28,000 ÷ ₹16,00,000 = 20.5%.**

**Why it differs.** Beta's implied required return on equity is lower than Alpha's because Beta uses less debt in its capital structure. As the equity capitalisation is a linear function of the debt-to-equity ratio under the net operating income approach, **the decline in required equity return offsets exactly the disadvantage of not employing so much in the way of 'cheaper' debt funds** — which is why both firms are worth the same ₹20,00,000.
keywords: linear function of the debt-to-equity ratio

mcqs.question: Under the net operating income approach, the apparent cheapness of debt is offset by:

options.A: A rise in the rate of interest on debt
options.B: A fall in earnings before interest and tax
options.C: An increase in the equity capitalisation rate, as investors are opposed to the greater risk from fixed return securities
options.D: An increase in the corporate tax rate

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.3: an increase in the use of debt, which is apparently cheaper, is offset by an increase in the equity capitalisation rate, because equity investors seek higher compensation as they are opposed to greater risk due to the existence of fixed return securities in the capital structure.

why_wrong.A: Kd is constant under this approach.
why_wrong.B: EBIT is given and unaffected by financing.

mcqs.trap: It is Ke, not Kd, that moves under NOI — the opposite of the traditional approach's later stage.

mcqs.question: A firm has net operating income of ₹5,00,000, debt of ₹15,00,000 at 10% and an overall cost of capital of 15%. Its cost of equity under the NOI approach is:

why_wrong.A: That is the overall cost of capital, not the cost of equity.
why_wrong.B: That is ₹3,50,000 ÷ ₹15,00,000, dividing by debt instead of equity.
why_wrong.C: That is the cost of debt.

mcqs.trap: Value the firm before you value the equity; the residual is the equity, not the other way round.

recap: NOI: capital structure is irrelevant; Ko and Kd are constant and Ke rises with leverage.
V = EBIT ÷ Ko; S = V − D; Ke = (EBIT − interest) ÷ S.
Cheaper debt is offset exactly by a dearer equity capitalisation rate.
Two firms with different gearing but the same NOI are worth the same.
